Manuscripts-turned AI agents can now 'talk' to each other and make new discoveries | Stanford University Medical Center, Tech Xplore

Since 1665, scholarly journals have served as written records of scientific advancement—static words on a page, references written by people for other people to read. That's about to change.

A team of Stanford Medicine researchers led by postdoctoral scholar Jiacheng Miao, Ph.D., and associate professor of biomedical data science James Zou, Ph.D., designed an artificial intelligence program called Paper2Agent that turns any scientific manuscript—including the text, figures and data—into an interactive AI agent that can chat about the paper and interact with other paper agents.

"For essentially all of human history, the way that we represent knowledge is in the form of these very passive artifacts," Zou said. "In earlier times people carved knowledge into stones, and now we type knowledge into words on pages—but in some sense pages aren't that much better."

Zou is programming a major update to the centuries-old practice of manuscript publishing. "This is an opportunity to fundamentally reimagine what knowledge looks like. Instead of having only passive artifacts, why don't we convert each static record into an active embodiment of knowledge?" Zou said. Think of it, he said, like a virtual author who knows how that knowledge is generated—one that's capable of explaining it and extending it by connecting with other papers and initiating new collaborations.

A paper describing the AI work has been published in Nature. Zou is the senior author, and Miao is the lead author.

Manuscripts manifested

The paper agents can answer questions about the work, apply methods from the paper to new data and even engage in conversations with other paper agents. The transformation from paper to AI agent starts with a team of bustling AI "worker agents" that pore over a single published paper and any associated code and data. But they're not just reading the paper. What's the best way to learn? Do it yourself.

The agents try to reproduce the original research from scratch. In a virtual environment, the agents simulate the research documented in the paper, and through that process, they capture the know-how a reader would otherwise have to dig out manually, from reagents needed to the experimental setup and execution.

The agents store that knowledge using something called an MCP, or model context protocol.

"An MCP lets AI essentially represent a paper PDF in a form that's easy for agents to access, almost like a filing system," Zou said. Each section of the paper is stored in a different folder, while the introduction, methods, results and conclusion are all organized into a separate file that lives in a parent file of a given paper.

AI does the heavy lifting, but Zou and the other human authors still have a role. The manuscript won't capture things like failed experiments or judgment calls behind experimental setups. So humans have to supply that context to the paper agent in conversational exchanges in which the agent can question the authors about the paper and research.

AI-to-AI collaboration

A "live-action" embodiment of knowledge can be a boon for readers of scientific manuscripts who seek to deeply understand the research, but these paper whisperers can do something even more impressive. They can talk to each other. That kind of agent-to-agent collaboration could become a vast research network—one with the potential to make real discoveries.

Zou and his team demonstrated the power of agent-to-agent collaboration by converting two unrelated papers into agents. One described a tool for predicting how genetic mutations affect the genome; the other described a genome-wide association study of the risk of developing attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

With both papers spun up into agents, the two began to find common ground. The genome prediction agent applied its knowledge to the ADHD dataset and flagged a molecular variant near a gene called MPHOSPH9 that's associated with increased ADHD risk—a connection that, according to Zou, had not been reported before.

"In the past, if there are two research groups that publish two different papers, those two research groups have to somehow find each other," Zou said. With paper agents, that overlap can surface without human legwork.

Zou's team chose these two initial papers and paired them for this demonstration, but the eventual goal, he said, is something closer to manuscript speed dating at scale: millions of paper agents surfacing common ground among themselves and working together to produce new insights.

Checking knowledge as it's built

Zou is careful to note that attribution still matters. Agents that extend a paper's reach are meant to help disseminate the original researchers' work, not obscure whose work it is. "It's still important to attribute the final discoveries and reference them back to original papers and original human authors," he said.

Zou also noted that the parameters under which agents collaborate—and make new discoveries—should be closely guided and monitored to ensure the agents' collaborations prioritize safety and ethical research.

The team is still expanding what a paper agent can do, including working out how, at scale, thousands or millions of these agents might productively find each other. Right now, the team has created more than 100 paper agents, but eventually, Zou hopes most manuscripts will have an associated paper agent. "Millions of papers are published every year," he said. "There's enormous potential here."

Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

HOW REVIEWERS CHECK YOUR JUSTIFICATIONS BEFORE GIVING YOU A QUALITY RATE

Reviewers, usually Quality Managers and experienced contributors, don’t just look at the score you gave. They also check the written explanation to make sure it shows real human reasoning. They use standard rubrics together with automated checks.

Here are the main things they look for:

1. EVIDENCE-BASED REASONING 📌

Don’t just make a claim without showing where you got it from.

For example, saying:

“Response A has a factual error.”

is not enough.

You should quote the exact part that is wrong and explain what the correct information should be, preferably with a reliable source when verification is needed.

Also, if the response failed to follow a particular instruction, mention exactly what it missed.

For example, if the user said “use 100 words maximum” and the response wrote 180 words, say that clearly instead of just saying “it did not follow the instructions.”

2. COMPARE BOTH RESPONSES PROPERLY ⚖️

One common mistake is reviewing Response A and Response B separately without actually comparing them.

If you choose “Much Better”, your explanation should make it clear why the difference is that big.

For example, a major factual error that changes the whole answer can justify a stronger preference. But if the only difference is that one response is slightly clearer, then “Slightly Better” may make more sense.

The important thing is that your written explanation should match the rating you selected.

3. CHECK THE ACTUAL RUBRIC 🎯

Your justification should touch on the important evaluation areas, such as:

Instruction Following:
Did the response follow all the user’s instructions, including small details and restrictions?

Truthfulness & Factuality:
Are the claims correct? If the answer depends on external facts, can they be verified from reliable sources?

Formatting & Presentation:
Did it follow the requested format, word count, markdown, code-block requirements, or other presentation instructions?

4. THINGS THAT CAN GET YOUR REVIEW FLAGGED 🚩

Rating Discrepancy:
If your explanation clearly says Response B is better but you select Response A on the rating slider, that can seriously hurt your review.

Vague Explanation:
Avoid statements like:

“Response A is more comprehensive, well-structured and helpful.”

That sounds nice, but it doesn’t actually explain why.

Mention the specific difference.

Too Much AI-Sounding Language:
Avoid repeatedly using phrases such as “delves into,” “in conclusion,” “it is important to note,” or writing overly polished, perfectly balanced paragraphs.

Your explanation should sound like a normal person who actually reviewed the two responses, not like you’re trying to write an academic paper.

Missing Constraints:
Always go back to the user’s original prompt. If there was a specific restriction, negative instruction, word limit, format, or required detail, check whether both responses followed it.

THE MAIN THING TO REMEMBER 🧠

Don’t just write what you feel about the responses.

Show what happened, where it happened, why it matters, and how it affects the comparison.

A good justification is basically:

Evidence → Problem/Strength → Comparison → Reason for the Rating

That is what makes your review look genuine and defensible.

Gen AI, AI agents, and agentic AI get used interchangeably, and the progression between them is actually a straight line: tool, then worker, then organization.

Gen AI generates content and stops there. A prompt goes in, text, image, or code comes out, tools like ChatGPT, Midjourney, and GitHub Copilot all fit here. The limitation is built into the design: one request, one response, no memory, no action taken on the world. It is a tool you operate, not something that operates on its own.

AI agents perceive, decide, and act. A goal goes in instead of a prompt, and the output is an action plus a result, not just text. Auto-GPT, a flight booking bot, or a debugging assistant all work this way, using tool use, memory, iteration, and self-correction to actually get something done rather than just describe it. The limitation is scope: this is still a single agent working alone, so anything bigger than one agent can handle stays out of reach.

Agentic AI orchestrates multiple agents at once. A complex objective goes in, and what comes out is a coordinated workflow, not one agent's output but several working together, the way a research team, a dev team, or a full business automation setup would. That requires multi-agent orchestration, consensus, delegation, and conflict resolution between agents that might disagree. The tradeoff is complexity, coordination overhead, and cost that a single agent never had to deal with.

The pattern underneath all three: a tool does what you tell it, a worker does what you goal it toward, an organization coordinates multiple workers toward something none of them could finish alone.

Bookmark this before you call a single chatbot agentic AI.
